To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
photolyases and their relatives cryptochromes are flavoproteins that use light to repair DNA damage or to transmit a signal.

the DNA photolyases are the only known proteins that can repair DNA damage by light and that cryptochromes are blue-light receptors that can regulate the plant and animal circadian clocks and are involved in the control of plant growth and development.
photolyases are highly conserved enzymes that repair photolesions in the DNA, that cryptochromes function as photoreceptor and that both photolyases and photoreceptors contain FAD as cofactor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis of the photolyases and related cryptochrome blue-light photoreceptors.
structural and mechanistic studies of DNA photolyase and cryptochrome proteins, and the elucidation of their biological functions.
the structural and functional characterization of photolyases, cryptochroms and their homologues, and the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of light-dependent DNA repair and photoreception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
structural information is still scarce, and that the molecular details of the repair and signaling reactions are not well understood.
the structural biology has provided a solid basis for understanding the molecular mechanism of DNA photorepair and cryptochrome function.
photolyase and cryptochrome proteins have a very complex and dynamic protein architecture that is crucial for their function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to solve the crystal structures of photolyase from Arabidopsis thaliana and from Escherichia coli, the latter in complex with DNA and a photolyase inhibitor.
we have been able to solve the structure of all photolyases and most cryptochromes from different species.
the structures have revealed the molecular mechanisms of the light-driven repair of UV-induced DNA lesions and of the light-dependent regulation of the biological clock.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cryptochromes have a similar architecture as photolyases, but the FAD cofactor in cryptochromes is bound in the same orientation as in the DNA repair enzyme.
the photolyase/cryptochrome family has evolved a highly conserved architecture that allows for the light-driven repair of DNA damage and blue-light photoreceptor function.

photolyases and their relatives have evolved from an ancestral DNA photolyase-like protein by a process of gene duplication and diversification that has resulted in a wide variety of proteins with a variety of biological functions.
